stories.headline: Trump waives most of the Russia sanctions law he signed a month ago
stories.dek: An Oct. 16 executive order suspends the tariffs and most sanctions of the Lindsey O. Graham Sanctioning Russia and Iran Act, using a waiver the statute itself provides, one that carries no congressional review period.
whatsNew: On Oct. 16, President Trump signed an executive order waiving the tariffs and most of the sanctions in the Lindsey O. Graham Sanctioning Russia and Iran Act of 2026 (H.R. 5334, Public Law 119-111), which he had signed into law on Sept. 18. [[c1]] The order waives all duties under sections 112 and 113 and the sanctions provisions of sections 102(a), 102(e) and 103 through 111, as well as section 117. [[c2]]
whyItMatters: The statute's tariff provisions use mandatory language: section 112 directs that, within 30 days of enactment, the President "shall" raise the duty on all goods imported from Russia, including oil and gas, to a rate of up to 500 percent. [[c3]] Section 113 sets a duty of up to 100 percent on goods from any country that was among the five largest importers of Russian crude oil or natural gas and keeps buying it. [[c4]] By the order's own terms, the 100 percent duty would have reached countries making new purchases of Russian oil or gas on or after Oct. 18. [[c5]]

The waived sections include sanctions on persons affiliated with the Russian government and on Russian financial institutions, a prohibition on investment by U.S. persons in Russia, a prohibition on energy exports to Russia and on purchases of Russian sovereign debt, and a ban on importing Russian uranium. [[c27]] The BBC notes that the law also targeted senior Russian figures, including Putin, and the "shadow fleet" of vessels used to get around existing embargoes. [[c28]]

The statute also contains a waiver: section 115 lets the President waive any sanction, restriction or duty in the title, provided he first sends Congress a written certification that the waiver is "in the national interests of the United States" and a report explaining the basis for it. [[c6]] The order states that this certification and report have been submitted. [[c7]] The law's congressional review mechanism is in section 117: under it, a full termination of sanctions cannot take effect for 30 calendar days, and Congress can block it by enacting a joint resolution of disapproval, while the waiver in section 115 requires only the certification and report. [[c8]] Among the provisions the order lists as waived is section 117 itself. [[c2]]

The order also hands the waiver power down the chain: it delegates the President's functions under section 115 to the Secretary of State, in consultation with the Treasury Secretary and the Trade Representative. [[c29]] Meeks had proposed amendments before passage, among them one "tightening the waiver language so President Trump would actually have to impose some of the sanctions." [[c30]] The cloture vote on the motion to proceed to the bill had passed the Senate 86-12 on July 28. [[c31]]

The waiver language was criticized before the vote: at a House Rules Committee hearing on Sept. 15, Rep. Gregory Meeks of New York, the ranking Democrat on the Foreign Affairs Committee, said "all of the sanctions in this bill can be waived at the president's discretion" and that there were "no safeguards around that waiver"; he also objected to giving the President broad new tariff authority. [[c9]] The Senate had passed the bill 86-11 on Aug. 7. [[c10]] The House agreed to the Senate version 262-159 on Sept. 16, with 203 Republicans and 58 Democrats in favor and 152 Democrats and 7 Republicans opposed. [[c11]]

The order does not undo everything: it states that sanctions imposed under earlier executive orders tied to the national emergency on Russia, which the President continued on March 24, 2026, are unaffected. [[c12]] The waivers remain in force until the President or the Secretary of State determines "that further action is appropriate." [[c13]] The order directs the U.S. Trade Representative to monitor purchases of Russian oil and gas and sanctions evasion and to inform the President of any circumstance that might call for further action, including on the waivers. [[c14]]

The administration's stated legal basis is the national-interest certification. [[c7]] CBS News and NBC News place the waiver in the context of energy prices: it came about a week after the President eased sanctions on Russian diesel and announced a deal with Vladimir Putin to bring Russian diesel to market. [[c15]] Kirill Dmitriev, an envoy to Putin, called the suspension "an important and truly historic moment." [[c16]] Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said the law "could have helped enormously." [[c17]]

Criticism in Congress came from both parties: Senate Democratic Leader Chuck Schumer said "there's nothing America First about Trump caving to Putin and exempting Russia from US sanctions." [[c18]] Sen. Thom Tillis (R-N.C.) called the decision "beyond irresponsible." [[c19]] Sen. Ted Cruz (R-Texas) said on Fox News that the decision was a mistake. [[c20]] Meeks said on Oct. 17: "Congress is not helpless." [[c21]]

Other Republicans joined in. Sen. John Cornyn (R-Texas) and Rep. Don Bacon (R-Neb.) both criticized the move, NBC News and the BBC reported; Bacon wrote that the President "is prolonging the war, not ending it." [[c32]] According to the BBC, Bacon also said many lawmakers will resist funding the President's agenda "knowing he is propping up a dictator's invasion." [[c33]] Sen. Richard Blumenthal (D-Conn.) called the waiver a "craven, cowardly action," NBC News reported. [[c34]] The administration has tied its Russia moves to fuel prices: the President is seeking to ease prices by tapping Russian energy, CBS News reported, and he has blamed Ukraine's strikes on Russian oil and gas infrastructure for higher fuel costs, according to NBC News. [[c35]]
whatsNext: No legislative response is scheduled before the election: the Senate is holding only pro forma sessions with no business expected and returns for business on Nov. 9. [[c22]] Meeks introduced H.R. 10828 on Oct. 15, a bill to impose sanctions on Russian oil and gas extraction and refinement; it was referred to Foreign Affairs and five other House committees. [[c23]] He says Congress "must also advance legislation fixing the Graham bill." [[c21]]

In the House, Meeks says his Ukraine Support Act has already passed with bipartisan support and that he introduced a bipartisan Prohibit Corrupt Russian Oil Deals Act this week. [[c21]] Zelenskyy said Ukrainian and U.S. negotiators spoke on Friday and that both teams could meet next week, the BBC reported. [[c36]] The order formally sets the 500 percent duty increase but makes it subject to the waivers, and the Trade Representative's monitoring is meant to flag any need for further presidential action. [[c37]]
background: H.R. 5334 began as a House tax bill on deductions for early-childhood educators; the Senate passed it with an amendment and a new title carrying the Russia sanctions. [[c24]] The law is named for the late Sen. Lindsey Graham; CBS News reported that he died before it was passed. [[c25]] Its sanctions division terminates five years after enactment. [[c26]]
The Senate had invoked cloture on the motion to proceed 86-12 on July 28 and passed the bill on Aug. 7. [[c31]]

stories.headline: Dec. 11 funding deadline awaits a lame-duck Congress
stories.dek: Government funding runs out five weeks after the midterms, none of the 12 full-year spending bills has passed the Senate, and the Nov. 3 result will shape what the current majority tries to do.
whatsNew: Congress has left Washington for the campaign with federal funding set to expire on Dec. 11 under the stopgap law enacted on Sept. 2 (H.R. 6500, Public Law 119-103). [[c1]] The Senate is holding only pro forma sessions and returns for business on Nov. 9. [[c2]] The House's next scheduled session is Oct. 19, according to the Clerk, and the Senate's pro forma sessions run on set days through Nov. 5. [[c15]]
whyItMatters: The continuing resolution keeps agencies covered by all 12 regular appropriations bills running from Oct. 1 through Dec. 11, a 72-day period. [[c3]] If Congress enacts neither full-year bills nor another stopgap by then, a funding gap begins on Dec. 12 that may lead to a shutdown of affected activities, the Congressional Research Service notes. [[c4]]

For most programs the stopgap provides funding at a rate based on the amounts, authorities and conditions of the fiscal 2026 appropriations acts, so agencies operate on last year's terms until Congress acts. [[c16]] The Senate's version, which became law, ran a week longer than the House's: to Dec. 11 instead of Dec. 4. [[c17]]

Little of the regular process is finished: the House Appropriations Committee reported all 12 fiscal 2027 bills and the House passed three, while the Senate Appropriations Committee had reported none, according to CRS. [[c5]] The three House-passed bills are Military Construction-Veterans Affairs (H.R. 8469, passed May 15), Agriculture-FDA (H.R. 8646, June 4) and National Security-State (Division A of H.R. 8595, July 15). [[c6]]

Other authorities tied to the same date include the fee authority under the Toxic Substances Control Act, which terminates on Dec. 11 unless Congress reauthorizes it. [[c18]] The law also bars the administration, through Dec. 11, from issuing or finalizing a proposed rule revising the government-wide "Uniform Guidance" for federal grants. [[c22]]

The deadline reaches beyond spending: the same law extends a set of expiring authorities only to Dec. 11, among them the Cybersecurity Information Sharing Act of 2015 and the Defense Production Act. [[c7]] The stopgap itself passed with wide margins, 90-6 in the Senate on Aug. 8 and 370-48 in the House on Sept. 1. [[c8]] The House had earlier passed its own version, H.R. 9770 from Appropriations Chair Tom Cole, which would have run only to Dec. 4, on a 220-205 vote. [[c9]]

Sen. Bernie Moreno (R-Ohio) told reporters on Oct. 15 that Republicans should stay in session to pass a party-line budget bill if they lose control of Congress, saying it would be "our last opportunity to pass something where we have unified control of government," Bloomberg Government reported. [[c10]] "We'll have turkeys here for Thanksgiving," he said. [[c10]] Judicial nominations are also queued for the post-election weeks: Bloomberg Law reported in September that action on nominees further back in the vetting pipeline would fall into the post-election calendar. [[c11]]

Republicans are looking at how to make further use of budget reconciliation, Bloomberg Government reported. [[c19]] Senate Majority Leader John Thune said in September that Republicans had "a big but limited opportunity to get some things done." [[c20]] Lame-duck confirmations may be harder because of attendance problems among outgoing senators, and Republican urgency will be greater if Democrats win, Bloomberg Law reported. [[c21]]
whatsNext: On Nov. 9, the Senate is scheduled to vote on cloture on the motion to proceed to H.R. 2347, the legislative vehicle for a permitting reform bill. [[c12]] The Senate's tentative calendar then sets aside Nov. 11-13 for Veterans Day and Nov. 23-27 for a Thanksgiving state work period, followed by a recess from Dec. 21. [[c13]] Before Dec. 11, Congress must pass the remaining appropriations or another continuing resolution to avoid a lapse in funding. [[c4]]
background: H.R. 6500 began as a House bill extending a trade preference program (the AGOA Extension Act) before the Senate turned it into the stopgap; such shells are a common vehicle for must-pass measures. [[c14]]

stories.headline: Justice Department sues California over mail ballots as Senate Democrats seek a non-interference pledge
stories.dek: Weeks before an election that decides control of Congress, the department is pressing state election officials over alleged noncitizen voters, and three Senate Democrats want a commitment that no ballots will be seized.
whatsNew: The Justice Department sued California on Oct. 15, asking a federal court to stop the state from counting mail ballots from more than 20,000 people the federal government identifies as likely noncitizens until their citizenship is confirmed. [[c1]] In a letter sent the same day, Sens. Alex Padilla (D-Calif.), Dick Durbin (D-Ill.) and Sheldon Whitehouse (D-R.I.) asked Attorney General Todd Blanche to commit that the department will not seize ballots, voting machines or other election materials in connection with the midterms. [[c2]]
whyItMatters: A handful of competitive House districts in California could help determine which party holds the House, the Associated Press noted. [[c3]]

The suit followed an Oct. 13 letter from McCotter that gave the state 48 hours to check a list of names and told officials to segregate the mail ballots of anyone whose citizenship could not be verified, warning that the department would otherwise "seek emergency relief." [[c16]] McCotter's later letter states that "noncitizen voting in a federal election is a federal crime." [[c5]] President Trump wrote on Truth Social that "they will all go to jail for a long period of time!!!" [[c17]]

"State-facilitated voter fraud is unacceptable in the United States of America," Blanche said in announcing it. [[c4]] The complaint says California "made no serious effort" to work with the federal government on identifying noncitizen registrants. [[c4]] On Oct. 16, a letter from Acting Deputy Attorney General Trent McCotter warned that officials who knowingly tabulate ballots from people flagged by federal agencies as noncitizens risk "becoming aiders and abettors to a federal crime," according to the AP, which obtained the letter. [[c5]]

The AP reported on an earlier federal claim about Nevada: the administration said Nevada had 1,500 noncitizen voters on its rolls, but the number of registered noncitizens turned out to be zero after the names were checked, the AP reported. [[c18]] Election law scholar Rick Hasen of UCLA said the new letter "ups the ante by threatening election officials with potential criminal prosecution." [[c19]] Assistant Attorney General Harmeet Dhillon sent letters to all 50 states in July threatening criminal action if they knowingly kept noncitizens on their rolls, CBS News reported. [[c20]]

Secretary of State Shirley Weber said the Department of Homeland Security had claimed over the summer that the state had 190,000 noncitizens on its rolls but would not provide its methodology or data sources. [[c6]] Los Angeles County Registrar Dean Logan declined to open the password-protected thumb drive the department sent with its list, saying it was not a secure device. [[c7]] The AP reported that the department has charged about 90 people this year for election misconduct, including 50 alleged noncitizen voters, against more than 227 million registered voters in 2024. [[c8]] The department's Civil Rights Division has filed 31 lawsuits seeking states' unredacted voter rolls. [[c9]]

Padilla is ranking member of the Senate Rules Committee, which has jurisdiction over federal elections, and Durbin is ranking member of the Judiciary Committee. [[c10]] Their letter says that "mail and absentee ballots have already been sent out to millions of voters" and that the department "has failed to affirm its election non-interference policy." [[c11]] Padilla says FBI Director Kash Patel committed under oath that the FBI would not seize ballots or voting equipment before an election is certified. [[c12]]

The letter builds on an earlier one: on June 8, Padilla, Durbin, Whitehouse and 21 other senators asked about the department's removal from its website of the Federal Prosecution of Election Offenses manual. [[c21]] The senators' release warns that "DOJ action that could spoil an election would be one of the most serious constitutional violations imaginable." [[c22]]
whatsNext: The senators asked whether any part of the department has developed or approved a plan to seize ballots, voting machines or other election materials relating to the 2026 elections. [[c13]] The lawsuit is before the U.S. District Court for the Central District of California. [[c14]] Logan said that "at this point, it is best for this to be addressed in court." [[c15]]

stories.headline: The FY2027 defense bill is stuck in the Senate, and the lame duck inherits it
stories.dek: The House passed its NDAA in July; the Senate has not begun debate since a failed cloture vote, and its first post-recess business is permitting reform.
whatsNew: The House passed H.R. 8800, the FY2027 National Defense Authorization Act, on July 22 by 216-212, and the bill was received in the Senate on September 14. [[c1]] [[c2]]

The Senate has not taken up either chamber's bill: its own version, S. 4784, was reported by the Armed Services Committee on June 15, and the last recorded step is a motion to proceed made on July 27. [[c3]] [[c6]]
whyItMatters: The vote that halted progress came on July 14, when cloture on the motion to proceed to S. 4784 failed 50-46 under a three-fifths threshold. [[c4]] Majority Leader John Thune voted no so that he could later move to reconsider, which keeps a second cloture vote available. [[c5]]

The two parties describe the impasse differently. Democratic Leader Chuck Schumer said: "Donald Trump is dragging America deeper into a war in Iran with no authorization, no plan, and no exit strategy. Democrats will not go along." [[c7]] Armed Services Chairman Roger Wicker said the objections "center on what is not in the bill," noting earlier votes on Iran and the committee's vote on the defense topline. [[c8]] He added that the bill would have carried 86 more amendments split evenly between the parties. [[c9]] Sen. Richard Blumenthal told NOTUS the NDAA "has become a referendum on the war." [[c14]]
The House bill is not a simple substitute vehicle: under the rule that governed it, the engrossed text sent to the Senate also included the Safeguard American Voter Eligibility Act. [[c10]]

An NDAA has been enacted every year for more than six decades, and the FY2026 act was described as the 65th in a row. [[c12]] CRS calculates that since FY1977 the bill has on average become law 45 days after the fiscal year began. [[c11]]
whatsNext: No Senate action on the NDAA is scheduled before the election. The Senate is holding only pro forma sessions until November 9, and its scheduled business that day is the motion to proceed to H.R. 2347, which the Senate Press Gallery's floor schedule describes as the legislative vehicle for the permitting reform bill, not the NDAA. [[c13]] Any Senate action on a defense bill would therefore come in the lame-duck session at the earliest, where leaders could retry cloture on S. 4784 or work from the House-passed H.R. 8800.
background: A motion to proceed is the Senate's vote on whether to take up a bill at all. Because that motion is itself debatable, the majority leader usually files cloture on it, which needs 60 votes. A failed cloture vote on the motion to proceed means debate on the bill never formally starts, so no amendments can be offered. [[c4]]

Entering a motion to reconsider is a routine tool: a senator who voted on the prevailing side can later ask the Senate to revisit the vote, which is why the majority leader often switches to no on a failed cloture vote. [[c5]]

stories.headline: Recess paperwork: three new laws, twelve bills to the President
stories.dek: With both chambers out, this week's legislative record consists of signatures and transmittals for bills the Senate cleared in late September.
whatsNew: Three Senate bills became law on October 15: S. 240, the Crow Tribe Water Rights Settlement Amendments Act (P.L. 119-122); S. 283, the Illegal Red Snapper and Tuna Enforcement Act (P.L. 119-123); and S. 2403, the Retire through Ownership Act (P.L. 119-124). [[c1]] [[c2]] [[c3]] Twelve House bills were presented to the President on October 14 and 15. [[c6]]
whyItMatters: None of these steps required a floor vote during the recess week. The three new laws had been presented to the President on October 5, and S. 2403 had cleared the House 401-14. [[c5]] [[c4]] The Senate itself met only in pro forma form; at its October 15 session no business was conducted. [[c11]]

Two of the House bills now awaiting enrollment carry foreign-policy and national-security weight. The Senate passed H.R. 1744, which reauthorizes the U.S. Commission on International Religious Freedom, by unanimous consent on September 29 after discharging the Foreign Relations Committee. [[c7]] It passed H.R. 9496, the End Tax Penalties on American Hostages Act, the same way on September 30. [[c8]] For both, the formal message on the Senate's action reached the House on October 14, the step that precedes enrollment and presentment. [[c9]]

Both bills had cleared the House without a recorded vote. H.R. 1744 passed by voice vote on June 8, after the Foreign Affairs Committee ordered it reported 45-0. [[c12]] [[c13]] H.R. 9496 passed by voice vote under suspension of the rules on September 15. [[c14]]
whatsNext: For the twelve bills already presented, the constitutional clock is running: the President has ten days, Sundays excepted, to sign or return a bill, or it becomes law without a signature unless an adjournment of Congress prevents its return. [[c10]] H.R. 1744 and H.R. 9496 still have to be enrolled and presented; the latest recorded action on each is the Senate's message to the House. [[c9]] Neither chamber is scheduled to vote again before Monday, November 9. [[c15]]
background: Unanimous consent lets the Senate pass a bill without a recorded vote if no senator objects; it is how most minor and many bipartisan bills clear the chamber. Discharging a committee by unanimous consent moves a bill to the floor without a committee report. [[c7]]

Suspension of the rules is the House's fast track: debate is limited to 40 minutes, no floor amendments are allowed, and passage requires two-thirds of those voting, which is why S. 2403's 401-14 vote is recorded as "2/3 required". [[c4]]

stories.headline: Cook moves 11 more House races toward Democrats, as its editor says Trump-won seats are 'in play'
stories.dek: The forecaster's second batch of shifts in a week leaves 16 Republican-held seats in its Toss Up column; ratings are forecasts, not results.
whatsNew: The Cook Political Report on Oct. 16 shifted 11 more House race ratings, all of them toward Democrats. [[c1]] Florida's open 16th District, Kansas's 2nd (Rep. Derek Schmidt) and Nebraska's 1st (Rep. Mike Flood) moved from Solid to Likely Republican. [[c2]] Five Republican-held seats moved from Likely to Lean Republican: Minnesota's 1st, Ohio's 10th and 15th, and the open 21st in New York and 1st in South Carolina; Montana's open 1st District moved into the Toss Up column. [[c3]] Two Democratic-held seats, Ohio's 1st and Florida's 25th, moved further toward Democrats. [[c14]] The batch follows 18 shifts toward Democrats that Cook announced on Oct. 9. [[c15]]
whyItMatters: The House currently has 218 Republicans, 214 Democrats, one independent and two vacancies, according to the Clerk of the House. [[c4]] All 435 seats are on the ballot on Nov. 3. [[c5]]

After the latest moves, Cook rates 185 seats Solid Democratic, 17 Likely Democratic, 12 Lean Democratic, 21 Toss Up, 13 Lean Republican, 16 Likely Republican and 171 Solid Republican. [[c6]] Of the 21 toss-ups, 16 are held by Republicans and five by Democrats. [[c7]] With the Oct. 9 changes, Cook said the most likely outcome was a Democratic gain of nine to 19 seats, which would give the party 224 to 234 seats. [[c8]] Cook's House editor Erin Covey wrote that scores of districts Donald Trump won by 10 or more points are now 'firmly in play.' [[c9]]
Ratings are expert judgments, not measurements: Cook bases them on district partisanship, candidate strength, the national environment and interviews with campaigns. [[c10]]
whatsNext: Speaker Mike Johnson told the AP he still expects Republicans to keep a working majority, adding: 'It's not going to be a giant majority.' [[c11]] Cook says the races it moved are drawing heavy outside spending from House Majority PAC, the Congressional Leadership Fund and MAGA Inc.'s super PACs. [[c12]] House Democratic leader Hakeem Jeffries is preparing a first-100-days agenda in case control changes. [[c13]]
background: Cook rates every House race on a seven-point scale from Solid Democratic to Solid Republican. 'Lean' races are competitive with one party favored; 'Toss Up' means either party has a good chance. A move from Solid to Likely signals that a seat has the potential to become engaged, not that it is expected to flip.

stories.headline: After failed war-powers votes, Iran war opponents look to the Dec. 11 funding deadline
stories.dek: The Senate has voted 14 times on ending U.S. hostilities with Iran; the one measure that cleared both chambers is a concurrent resolution the administration treats as non-binding, which moves the debate toward the power of the purse.
whatsNew: The Senate's most recent Iran war-powers vote failed on September 24, when it rejected H.Con.Res. 89 by 49-50 [[c1]]. Four Republicans, Susan Collins, Lisa Murkowski, Rand Paul and Thom Tillis, voted yes, while Democrat John Fetterman voted no [[c2]]. Government funding under current law runs through December 11 [[c10]].
whyItMatters: The record shows how far these efforts have gotten under the War Powers Resolution, and where they stop. The Senate has held 14 roll-call votes this year on measures to remove U.S. forces from hostilities with Iran; two succeeded: a motion to discharge S.J.Res. 185 on May 19 and adoption of H.Con.Res. 86 on June 23 [[c4]]. H.Con.Res. 86, sponsored by Rep. Gregory Meeks, passed the House 215-208 on June 3 and the Senate 50-48 on June 23 [[c3]].

The form of that measure is the crux. Section 5(c) of the War Powers Resolution provides for a concurrent resolution, which passes both chambers but is not sent to the president [[c18]]. The Congressional Research Service notes that the Supreme Court's 1983 decision in INS v. Chadha found such resolutions, when they approve or disapprove executive action, unconstitutional because they are not presented to the president [[c7]]. Congress answered the same year with a second fast-track route: a joint resolution or bill, which the president can veto and which then needs a two-thirds majority in each chamber [[c8]]. That is why most Senate votes this year were on joint resolutions, and why none of them became law [[c4]].

The two branches read the June vote differently. In its statement of administration policy on H.Con.Res. 86, the White House Office of Management and Budget said that concurrent resolutions such as H.Con.Res. 86 lack the force of law and should be deemed unconstitutional legislative vetoes [[c6]]. Meeks says the measure is binding under the War Powers Resolution and that he will explore legal avenues to ensure the executive complies [[c9]]. No court has ruled on that dispute, so the legal effect of the June vote is contested.

The votes have entered the campaign debate. Collins, who is seeking re-election in Maine, voted yes on nine of the 14 Senate votes [[c5]]. She has defended her earlier no votes by saying a commander-in-chief has wide discretion during the first 60 days of a conflict, while Rep. Ashley Hinson, the Republican Senate nominee in Iowa, said in a debate that another floor resolution was not needed to end the war, Responsible Statecraft reported [[c11]]. For students of Congress, the episode shows the contrast between measures passed by majorities and the two-thirds of each chamber needed to override a veto of a joint resolution [[c8]].
whatsNext: The next fixed date is the expiry of the current stopgap. H.R. 6500 became Public Law 119-103 on September 2 and funds the government through December 11 [[c10]]. A funding limit written into an appropriations law would, unlike the June resolution, go to the president for signature or veto [[c8]].

Whether opponents of the war will use that deadline is not settled. Responsible Statecraft reported that some Democratic senators have said they would use a Senate majority to block future Defense Department funding until the war is over [[c12]]. The Intercept, a left-leaning outlet, describes the December 11 expiration as an opportunity to attach a rider barring funds for the war, while noting that the price could be a shutdown [[c13]]. Neither report describes a decision by party leaders.

Military planning continues in parallel. CBS News reported, citing unnamed sources, that the White House and Pentagon have prepared plans to use the largest U.S. non-nuclear bomb against Iranian military sites if ordered; a White House spokesperson said the administration does not comment on such plans [[c14]]. According to the same report, Trump said last week that the U.S. would not attack Iran before the midterm elections [[c15]].
background: The War Powers Resolution of 1973 requires the president to report to Congress after introducing forces into hostilities; 60 days after that report, the use of force is to end unless Congress authorizes it, with a possible 30-day extension [[c16]].
H.Con.Res. 89, sponsored by Rep. Pramila Jayapal, was a near-identical successor to H.Con.Res. 86; it passed the House 214-208 on July 23 before failing in the Senate on September 24 [[c17]] [[c1]].

stories.headline: Senate Democrats file a resolution to block the U.S.-Saudi nuclear deal, setting up a vote after Nov. 29
stories.dek: S.J.Res. 221 uses the Atomic Energy Act's review procedure, under which a nuclear cooperation agreement takes effect unless Congress enacts a disapproval, and the resolution would be subject to a presidential veto.
whatsNew: Sens. Jeff Merkley and Edward Markey introduced S.J.Res. 221 on October 15, a joint resolution stating that Congress does not favor the U.S.-Saudi agreement for civilian nuclear cooperation that the president transmitted on September 14 [[s1]]. The measure was referred to the Foreign Relations Committee under a Senate order of September 30 [[s2]], and its sponsors say it sets up a Senate vote after November 29 [[s3]].
whyItMatters: Section 123 of the Atomic Energy Act puts the burden on opponents. A cooperation agreement does not need Congress's approval; it is blocked only if, during a sixty-day review period, Congress adopts and there is enacted a joint resolution stating that it does not favor the agreement [[s4]]. The statute adds a separate thirty-day submission period of continuous session, which is why the sponsors speak of a 90-day review after which the agreement takes effect unless Congress acts [[s5]].

The word 'enacted' matters. A joint resolution goes to the president, who can veto it [[s6]]. The administration is on record supporting the agreement: in Presidential Determination No. 2026-18 of July 16, Trump found that it 'will promote, and will not constitute an unreasonable risk to, the common defense and security' and approved it [[s7]]. Energy Secretary Chris Wright and Saudi Energy Minister Prince Abdulaziz bin Salman signed the 123 agreement together with a bilateral safeguards agreement, and Wright said the agreements 'uphold the highest standards of nuclear safety and nonproliferation' [[s8]].

The substantive dispute is about enrichment and inspections. Merkley and Markey argue that the agreement lacks the so-called gold standard, under which a partner forgoes enrichment and reprocessing, and the IAEA Additional Protocol, which allows more intrusive inspections [[s9]]. NBC News reported, citing three people familiar with the agreement, that it was not expected to include a ban on enrichment or reprocessing, and the Arms Control Association reported that, according to the text of the deal, the United States will support Saudi Arabia's decision to develop enrichment without requiring a more intrusive IAEA safeguards agreement [[s10]]. The sponsors also argue that the United Arab Emirates, which accepted both conditions, could seek to renegotiate its own agreement if Saudi Arabia gets more favorable terms [[s11]]. Markey summarized his position by saying the deal 'is about megatons, not megawatts' [[s15]]. The sponsors add a regional argument: Iran, they say, would reject future limits that Saudi Arabia was not held to, and they point to Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman's statement that the kingdom would develop a nuclear weapon if Iran acquired one [[s17]]. Merkley framed the vote as a test of Congress's own role, saying 'we can't sleepwalk into a decision this consequential' and that the law gives Congress the power to review and block such a deal [[s16]].

The case also shows how the review works: a 123 agreement takes effect unless a joint resolution of disapproval is enacted, and because it must be enacted, the resolution is subject to a presidential veto [[s4]] [[s6]].
whatsNext: The statute directs the Senate Foreign Relations and House Foreign Affairs committees to hold hearings during the sixty-day period and to report whether the agreement should be approved or disapproved [[s13]]. The sponsors expect a Senate vote after November 29, after the midterm elections [[s3]]. The Arms Control Association expects pushback from legislators of both parties but considers it unclear whether there is enough opposition to pass a disapproval resolution [[s18]].

One political variable is the link to Israel. According to the Arms Control Association, Trump posted that the agreement 'will be approved, but is totally subject to Saudi Arabia joining' the Abraham Accords, while the sponsors say the agreement itself contains no formal requirement of that kind [[s12]]. If no disapproval is enacted before the review period ends, the agreement can take effect [[s4]].
background: The exact end of the review clock is not public in a primary source we could check. The resolution refers to a transmittal on September 14 [[s1]], while the Arms Control Association reported a submission on Aug. 24 [[s14]]; periods under the statute are counted in days of continuous session, which pause during long adjournments [[s5]].

stories.headline: Bipartisan senators, four of them Republicans, ask the Pentagon's inspector general to investigate Ukraine's Starshield disruption
stories.dek: Nine senators want to know whether U.S. officials approved or knew in advance of restrictions on the military satellite service, and whether SpaceX acted on its own.
whatsNew: Nine senators sent a letter on October 15 to the Defense Department's inspector general, Platte Moring III, calling for an investigation into the disruption of U.S.-maintained Starshield systems used by Ukraine [[t1]]. The letter was led by Thom Tillis and Jeanne Shaheen, the co-chairs of the Senate NATO Observer Group, and is signed by four Republicans and five Democrats [[t3]] [[t2]].
whyItMatters: The letter is oversight of the executive branch that includes members of the president's own party among its signers, using an inspector general rather than a committee hearing. Its central question is who decided: the senators ask whether Defense Department or other U.S. officials directed, authorized, approved or had advance knowledge of changes to intelligence-sharing, warning capabilities or Starlink and Starshield services affecting Ukraine [[t4]]. They also ask whether SpaceX imposed restrictions on its own and whether that complied with U.S. government contracts [[t5]], and whether U.S. personnel, the U.S. Embassy in Kyiv and Ukrainian authorities received adequate advance notice of the changes [[t16]].

The Republican signers are Tillis, Susan Collins, John Cornyn and Lisa Murkowski; the Democrats are Shaheen, Dick Durbin, Jack Reed, Chris Coons and Richard Blumenthal [[t2]]. The list includes committee leaders: Reed is the top Democrat on the Armed Services Committee, and Collins chairs the Appropriations Committee and sits on the Intelligence Committee [[t17]]. The senators frame the issue as one of protecting Americans as well as supporting Ukraine: they write that they are alarmed by incidents in which U.S. diplomatic, military and security personnel could not reach designated bunkers during Russian air raids [[t6]]. They also point to the contract structure, writing that some of the services are provided through arrangements administered by the U.S. Space Force and that Ukraine previously had unlimited speeds [[t7]]. By their own account, the cause of the incidents remains unclear [[t15]], which is why the letter also asks what immediate corrective measures are being taken so that American personnel in Ukraine receive reliable threat warnings [[t20]].

The accounts of the disruption differ. Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy has said speed restrictions hindered Ukraine's ability to intercept Russian drones, Stars and Stripes reported, and called the loss of access a 'big mistake,' according to The Hill [[t9]]. SpaceX owner Elon Musk wrote that Starshield is owned and controlled by the U.S. government, with limits set by the military and ultimately the president [[t10]]. President Trump denied limiting Ukraine's access, saying 'it wasn't me,' the BBC reported [[t11]], and Stars and Stripes reported that the U.S. has denied cutting back intelligence-sharing with Ukraine [[t12]]. The Hill reported that access was quickly restored [[t13]]. Stars and Stripes placed the episode in a period of tension between Zelenskyy and Trump after Trump announced a deal to import Russian diesel [[t18]].

An inspector general request is an oversight route outside committee hearings: senators can ask, but the inspector general decides what to investigate. Tillis, who first called for an inspector general review on Wednesday evening, according to The Hill [[t19]], said he was 'not holding my breath' for Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth to offer transparency, according to The Hill [[t14]].
whatsNext: The senators ask the inspector general to confirm the status of an investigation in writing and to provide an initial briefing no later than November 1 [[t8]]. Whether the office opens a review, and how broad it is, will show whether the question of who ordered the restriction can be answered through oversight. The letter does not say what the signers would do without a response; Collins chairs the Appropriations Committee [[t17]].
